purpose: Editorial recommendation metadata and inspected-source provenance for P07, P09, and P10. Together with the earlier P08 draft, these complete the precision and economy family. Fields remain outside strict Commons frontmatter.

articles.title: Choose the Specific Word
use_when: A broad label leaves the relevant condition or distinction unnamed.
A forceful synonym changes the claim or imports an unsupported cause.
More detailed wording may be unnecessary for the passage's purpose or viewpoint.
mechanisms: Naming the property relevant to the reader's purpose
Comparing the implications of near synonyms
not_ideal_when: The evidence supports only a broad or qualified description.
A narrow classification would distract from the purpose or exceed the viewpoint's knowledge.
example_user_queries: My editor says the wording is vague but I do not know what to change.
I have said something is damaged without explaining what is wrong with it.
How specific should a description be?
The stronger word sounds better but may claim more than I know.
I keep choosing synonyms that subtly change the tone.
Do I need the exact species or material name in every description?
How can I distinguish what I observed from what I think caused it?
My description tells readers that something is bad but not why.
A character label seems to settle a feeling I want to leave open.
Can a longer phrase be more precise than a single vivid word?

sources.author: UNC Writing Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
sources.title: Word Choice
sources.inspected_material: The sections on inaccurate word meanings, unwanted connotations and broad or loaded wording, plus the strategies cautioning that thesaurus synonyms have different shades of meaning.
sources.supports: Selecting wording for its actual meaning and connotations rather than treating near synonyms as interchangeable or assuming a broader label explains the intended distinction.
sources.limits: The bookshop and farewell-party situations are original. The observation/inference boundary, purpose-dependent specificity, and distinction from selecting a revealing detail are editorial development; no source exercise, full book passage, or empirical effect is claimed.

visual_decision.implementation: Developed prose comparisons expose the meaningful differences in wording and interpretation. No separate table, diagram, illustration, or interactive practice is needed.

articles.title: Cut Redundancy
use_when: Several sentences rephrase the same point without developing it.
Merged drafts duplicate explanations or background.
Cutting risks losing a qualification or useful repetition along with excess wording.
mechanisms: Comparing the work performed by phrases and passages
Retaining distinctions and claim boundaries during compression
Judging recurrence by its function rather than its surface wording
not_ideal_when: Recurrence provides needed orientation, emphasis, rhythm, or emotional development.
A proposed deletion would remove evidence, a material limit, or the actual meaning of the claim.
example_user_queries: My paragraph says the same thing in several different ways.
How can I shorten this without losing the nuance?
I combined drafts and now the background appears twice.
My argument feels long but never seems to move forward.
Should I remove every repeated word?
A shorter rewrite sounds more certain than the original.
I cannot tell whether this sentence develops the point or just repeats it.
My story repeats an action and I am unsure whether the repetition earns its place.
How do I keep useful reminders without explaining everything again?
I cut the qualifications and now the claim seems too broad.

sources.author: Purdue OWL, Purdue University
sources.title: Concision
sources.inspected_material: The opening distinction between effective wording and the fewest words, and section 2 on checking each word for a useful contribution.
sources.supports: Evaluating economy by the work wording performs rather than minimizing word count alone.
sources.limits: No Purdue exercise is reproduced or adopted as a claim of exact semantic equivalence. Rehearsal-space, project-trial, and narrative examples are original; no measured readability effect is asserted.

sources.author: UNC Writing Center, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
sources.title: Word Choice
sources.inspected_material: The section Selecting and using key terms, specifically Repetition vs. redundancy.
sources.supports: Distinguishing useful repetition of stable key terms from repeatedly restating an undeveloped point.
sources.limits: The scale distinctions, qualification-preserving comparisons, and emotional narrative example are editorial development rather than reproduced source passages.

visual_decision.implementation: Developed prose comparisons expose the meaningful differences in wording and interpretation. No separate table, diagram, illustration, or interactive practice is needed.

articles.title: Choose Terms the Reader Can Use
use_when: Unexplained terms or local shorthand prevent the intended reader from acting.
Expanding an abbreviation still leaves its concept or consequence unclear.
Simplification would erase a technical distinction the audience needs.
mechanisms: Matching vocabulary to audience and task
Connecting a necessary term to an example, contrast, or consequence
Introducing and then consistently reusing a useful label
not_ideal_when: The audience already knows the term and an explanation would interrupt its task.
A substituted ordinary word would collapse a distinction essential to the instruction.
example_user_queries: My instructions are accurate but newcomers do not know what to do.
How much jargon can I keep for a mixed audience?
I expanded the acronym and readers still do not understand the sentence.
Replacing a technical term with a simple word seems to lose an important distinction.
Should I explain this term here or put it in a glossary?
I cannot tell which words my readers already know.
Our team uses ordinary words with meanings that outsiders do not recognize.
I want readers to learn the term because they will encounter it again.
Does plain language mean explaining every abbreviation?
How can I check whether a definition actually helps someone complete the task?

sources.author: Australian Government Style Manual
sources.title: Plain language and word choice
sources.inspected_material: The sections Learn about the words people use and Keep words and phrases with special meaning to a minimum, including audience research, specialist vocabulary, explanations, and selective shortened forms.
sources.supports: Choosing vocabulary in relation to audience knowledge and explaining or retaining specialist terms according to actual reader need.
sources.limits: No claim about a statutory accessibility threshold is made. Studio and workplace processes are invented and locally defined; they are not universal technical procedures.

sources.author: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Clear Communication Index
sources.title: Does the material always use words the primary audience uses?
sources.inspected_material: The guidance on audience vocabulary, explaining unfamiliar terms at the point of use, testing understanding, and selective explanation of abbreviations.
sources.supports: Explaining unfamiliar language where it becomes necessary and checking what the intended audience actually understands.
sources.limits: The source supports communication guidance only. No health recommendation, health example, quantified processing effect, or validated result for the invented explanations is claimed.

visual_decision.implementation: Developed prose comparisons expose the meaningful differences in wording and interpretation. No separate table, diagram, illustration, or interactive practice is needed.
